To enable the fluence model, you must do a number of things:
•
You must identify the particle species on a RADIATION statement. Available species are 
ALPHA, ELECTRON, ION, NEUTRON, PHOTON, PROTON, and USER (for user-defined 
particles).
•
On a MATERIAL statement, you must specify values for the material-specific properties, 
namely the damage factor, the non-ionizing energy loss, and the DENSITY.
•
You must set the FLUENCE.MODEL flag on a DEFECTS statement, and specify the 
interaction cross-sections for the defects.
•
You must specify a value for the FLUENCE on the RADIATION statement for the particle in 
question, or on a subsequent SOLVE statement.
Victory Device allows you to specify combinations of particle species, with a separate fluence 
for each type. If you do this, each species must have its own RADIATION statement.

p_0b1d177a0b.title: 6.5.1  Material Damage Parameters
p_0b1d177a0b.content:
6.5.1  Material Damage Parameters
In the fluence model, the creation of defect states is affected by three material properties: the 
damage factor, the non-ionizing energy loss, and the mass density.
D
The damage factor (
) expresses the number of defect states created per unit energy
deposited in the material. In Victory Device it has units of defect-states/MeV. It is specific to 
the type of irradiating particle and to the material itself. Accordingly, the MATERIAL
statement has a damage factor parameter for each particle species. For example, the damage 
factor for alpha particles is specified by the DAMAGE.ALPHA parameter, and the parameters 
for the other particle types follow a similar naming pattern. They are listed in Table 13-158.
A quantity called the linear stopping power expresses the rate at which energy is lost by an 
irradiating particle per unit distance it travels in a given material. Because the value of the 
linear stopping power is approximately proportional to the material mass density, one often 
considers instead the ratio of these two quantities, which is termed the mass stopping power. 
The component of the mass stopping power that does not involve ionizing interactions is 
called the non-ionizing energy loss (NIEL). In Victory Device, the non-ionizing energy loss 
(
) has units of MeV·cm2/(g·particle). You specify it by assigning a value to the
EL
DAMAGE.NIEL parameter on a MATERIAL statement.

Confidential
Lattice Dislocation Defects
Radiation Effects Module (REM)
The remaining material parameter appearing in Equation 6-49 is the mass density, which is 
simply the mass per unit volume of the given material. In Victory Device, it has units of g/
cm3. You specify it by assigning a value to the DENSITY parameter on a MATERIAL statement.

p_438dcc1d5c.title: 6.5.2  Defect Parameters
p_438dcc1d5c.content:
6.5.2  Defect Parameters
The defect states created when the FLUENCE.MODEL flag is set on a DEFECTS statement are 
similar to the inherent defect states described when the flag is not set, but there are a few 
differences.
To start with, when the FLUENCE.MODEL flag is set, the density of defect states is calculated 
using Equation 6-49, instead of being declared explicitly. Except as noted below, this density 
applies individually to both acceptor-like and donor-like defect states. The energy levels of 
these defect states are assumed to be uniformly distributed across the bandgap.
As with inherent defects, the NUMA and NUMD parameters on the DEFECTS statement specify 
the number of energy levels used to represent the distribution of acceptor-like and donor-like 
defects states respectively. If you want to describe only defects of a single type, you must 
explicitly set the number of levels for the other type to zero.
When the FLUENCE.MODEL flag is set, the tail-state parameters SIGTAE, SIGTAH, SIGTDE, 
and SIGTDH are used to specify the cross-sections. However, because the defect energy levels 
are distributed uniformly across the bandgap, the decay energies WTA and WTD are not used, 
and neither are any of the Gaussian parameters.

p_2331821dee.title: 6.5.3  Particle Fluence
p_2331821dee.content:
6.5.3  Particle Fluence
A fluence is the accumulation of a flux over time, so when we refer to a particle fluence we 
mean all of the particles that have ever passed through a given cross-sectional area. In Victory 
Device, the particle fluences have units of particles/cm2.
In setting up the radiation fluence model, you can specify an initial FLUENCE for a given 
particle on its corresponding RADIATION statement. If you do not specify an initial fluence, it 
will be set to zero. On subsequent SOLVE statements, you can update these fluence values. In 
Victory Device, the SOLVE statement has fluence parameters for each available particle 
species, so you can set the fluence value for each species independently. These fluence-setting 
parameters are listed in Table 6-5.

p_72a645c1c9.title:
Chapter 7 
Optoelectronic Simulation
p_72a645c1c9.content:
Chapter 7 
Optoelectronic Simulation
User-Defined Photogeneration Models
Optoelectronic Simulation
Victory Device includes support for modeling light-sensitive semiconductor devices. These 
models add to the electron/hole generation, depending on the light absorbed in the structure. 
The BEAM statement specifies an optical input signal in the form of a collimated beam of light. 
You can have up to 10 beams (numbered 1 to 10). Each beam has an associated 
photogeneration model and an intensity. Beam intensities for these 10 beams are set on a 
SOLVE statement using the B<number> parameter. The actual photogeneration models and 
associated parameters are set on a BEAM statement. These models can either be user-defined 
models implemented using the C-Interpreter, or ray-tracing models.

p_8333e15587.title: 7.1  User-Defined Photogeneration Models
p_8333e15587.content:
7.1  User-Defined Photogeneration Models
Victory Device provides two C-Interpreter functions that allow you to define your own 
photogeneration models (see Appendix A C-Interpreter Functions). The names of files 
containing these functions are identified by parameters on a BEAM statement.
The function radiate(), read from the file identified by the F.RADIATE parameter, allows 
you to define a photogeneration rate that may depend on position and time. The function 
irradiate(), read from the file identified by the F.IRRADIATE parameter, allows you to 
define a photogeneration rate that may depend on position, time, and the electric field. You 
may specify one or the other of these parameters on a BEAM statement, but not both.
During a solution, the output from these functions will be multiplied by the optical intensity 
specified on a SOLVE statement. The optical intensity is in W/cm2, so to get the generation 
rate in the required units of cm3s1, the output of the functions radiate() and 
irradiate() must be in units of W1cm1s1.
For example:
BEAM NUMBER=1 F.RADIATE=my_file.c  
BEAM NUMBER=2 F.IRADIATE=my_file.c
SOLVE B1=0.1 B2=1.5
This would set beam 1 and beam 2 to be based on a pair of functions
int radiate(double x, double y, double z, double t, double *rat)
and
int irradiate(double x,  double y,  double z,  double t,
              double ex, double ey, double ez, double *rat)
both of which are defined in the file 'my_file.c'.
Victory Device would then apply beams 1 and 2 multiplied by the intensity factors 0.1 and 1.5 
respectively to the simulation.

p_ba7b7198a0.title: 13.30.3  Description
p_ba7b7198a0.content:
13.30.3  Description
The OUTPUT statement provides control over which extra variable will be written to structure 
files. Each of the possible flags triggers the output of specific quantities as described below. 
All flags are optional and may be arbitrarily combined. Parameters specified by the flags on 
an OUTPUT statement will be stored in the standard-format structure files output by 
subsequent SOLVE and SAVE statements, in addition to data that Victory Device stores in such 
structure files by default.
Data in structure files is represented at the nodes of the structural mesh. Certain quantities are 
calculated in Victory Device along the links or edges between nodes. When output to a 
structure file, such quantities are interpolated to the nodal points. They may also be subjected 
to various operations, such as averaging, filtering, and projection. Directional quantities 
treated in this manner include the current densities, electric field, and mobilities.

p_1bbe5abe44.title: 13.34  PROBE
p_1bbe5abe44.content:
13.34  PROBE
PROBE  allows you to output the value of several distributed quantities to the log file. For 
point probes, the value of the probed quantity at the specified location will be saved to the log 
file at each bias or time point. For non-point probes, the value saved can be the minimum, 
maximum, integrated, or average value within a specified area of the device.

p_9ed9f96466.title: 13.34.1  Syntax
p_9ed9f96466.content:
13.34.1  Syntax
PROBE location-type quantity [localization] 
      [NAME=name] [FILENAME=filestem] [SCALE=value]
      [COMPLIANCE] [PRINT] [max-file]
The probe location-type identifies either a particular point, or a distributed function:
location-type: xyz | POSITION=coordinate-string |
               AVERAGE | INTEGRATED | MAXIMUM | MINIMUM
For point probes, the coordinates of the probe position can be specified individually
xyz: [X=value] [Y=value] [Z=value]
or in a coordinate string. A coordinate-string consists of an ordered-pair (in 2D) or ordered-
triplet (in 3D) of real numbers, representing the positional coordinates in m. For example:
POSITION="(0.5,0.5,0.0)"
Quantities that may be probed include primary variables, species variables, and certain 
scalars, vectors, and tensors:
quantity: primary | species | scalar | vector | mobility | user
The basic primary variables are:
primary: POTENTIAL | N.CONC | P.CONC | 
         LAT.TEMP  | N.TEMP | P.TEMP
Concentrations of mobile species are also primary. Except for the ion mobility, the remaining 
species variables are scalars.
species: conc-sp | react-sp | trap-sp | ft-sp
conc-sp: SPECIES="species-name" | SPECIES1 | SPECIES2 | SPECIES3
react-sp: REACTION.SPECIES="species-name" |
          REACTION.SP1 | REACTION.SP2 | REACTION.SP3
trap-sp: SPECIES.TRAPPING="species-name" |
         U.SP1TRAP | U.SP2TRAP | U.SP3TRAP
ft-sp: FT.SPECIES="species-name" | (FT.MSC MSC.STATE=n)
The other scalars that may be probed are:
scalar: BAND.GAP | CONDUCTION.BAND | VALENCE.BAND |
        GR.HEAT | JOULE.HEAT | PT.HEAT | TOTAL.HEAT | AUGER | 
        GEMINATE.YIELD | GENERATION | LANGEVIN | PHOTOGEN |
        R.BBT | RADIATION.GENERATION | RECOMBINATION | RADIATIVE | 
        SRH | E.TRANTRAP | H.TRANTRAP | CHARGE | PERMITTIVITY | 
        QFN | QFP | TOTAL DOSE |PP.AVALANCHE | PE.AVALANCHE | 
        PH.AVALANCHE | ALPHAN | ALPHAP | ACCEPTOR.TRAPS | 
        DONOR.TRAPS | INTERFACE.ACCEPTOR.TRAPS |

Confidential
PROBE
Statements
INTERFACE.DONOR.TRAPS | INCOMPLETE.DONOR | 
        INCOMPLETE.ACCEPTOR | LKCHARGE | LKSTATE | 
        AMP.TRAP | CONCAMP.PTRAP | CONCAMP.0TRAP | CONCAMP.NTRAP
        BQP.N | BQP.P | CONDUCTIVITY | ELECTRON.AFFINITY | 
        RESISTIVITY | SONOS.CHARGE | CAPT.N.CONC | CAPT.P.CONC |
        CAPT.SRH | CAPT.AUGER | CAPT.TRAP | CAPT.OPTR | 
        MZ.HEAVYHOLE | MT.HEAVYHOLE | MZ.LIGHTHOLE | MT.LIGHTHOLE | 
        MZ.SPLITOFFHOLE | MT.SPLITOFFHOLE | MZ.ELECTRON | 
        MT.ELECTRON | R.NLEBBT | R.NLHBBT | E.T2CRATE | H.T2CRATE
Vector quantities take the form:
vector: vec-param 
       [component | ([DIR] [POLAR]) | ([THETA] [ZETA])] |
       VEL.ELECTRON | VEL.HOLE
For vectors,
vec-param: FIELD | J.CONDUCTION | J.ELECTRON |
              J.HOLE | J.TOTAL | ALPHAN.VEC | 
              ALPHAP.VEC | FERRO.PERMITTIVITY | 
              FERRO.POLARIZATION |PREISACH.PERMITTIVITY | 
              PREISACH.POLARIZATION | VEL.ELECTRON |
              VEL.HOLE |
component: V.MAG | V.X | V.Y | V.Z | 
               V.XANG | V.ZANG | V.THETA | V.ZETA
Mobility-related quantities take the form:
mobility: mob-param [mob-direction]
For mobilities,
mob-param: N.MOB | P.MOB | ION.MOBILITY=species-name
mob-direction: V.MAG | V.X | V.Y | V.Z | 
              ([DIR] [POLAR]) | ([THETA] [ZETA])
User parameters are used to add manually managed quantities to a log file. These take the 
form:
user:  USER1 | USER2 | USER3 | USER4
Probes may be localized to a particular material or region. Additionally or alternatively, they 
may be localized to a specified box, cylinder, or polygonal prism:
localization: [MATERIAL=material | REGION=n | RNAME=region-name] 
              [box | cylinder | prism]
box: [X.MINIMUM=value] [X.MAXIMUM=value]
     [Y.MINIMUM=value] [Y.MAXIMUM=value]
     [Z.MINIMUM=value] [Z.MAXIMUM=value]
cylinder: [R.MINIMUM=value] [R.MAXIMUM=value]
          [A.MINIMUM=value] [A.MAXIMUM=value]
          [Z.MINIMUM=value] [Z.MAXIMUM=value]
prism: POLYGON=coord-string
       [ (X.MINIMUM=value X.MAXIMUM=value) |

Confidential
PROBE
Statements
(Y.MINIMUM=value Y.MAXIMUM=value) |
         (Z.MINIMUM=value Z.MAXIMUM=value) ]
A grid of the maximum probe values in a specified direction may be saved to a CSV file.
max-file: [DX.MAX.FILE=value] [DY.MAX.FILE=value]
          [DZ.MAX.FILE=value] [DIR.X.MAX.FILE] 
          [DIR.Y.MAX.FILE]    [DIR.Z.MAX.FILE] 
          [DIRECTION]         [MAX.FILE]

p_7b1fe97fc4.title: 13.34.2  Examples
p_7b1fe97fc4.content:
13.34.2  Examples
Probing a Maximum Value
The following command will cause the maximum electron concentration in silicon regions to 
be output to the log file.
PROBE MAX N.CONC MATERIAL=silicon NAME="Peak Electrons"
Probing at a Point
The following command will cause the potential at the indicated position to be output to the 
log file, scaled so that the value is in millivolts.
PROBE X=0.25 Y=0.5 POTENTIAL SCALE=1000 NAME="Potential (mV)"
Probing for a Vector Quantity
For vector quantities, you can only probe for a single scalar component per PROBE statement. 
The component is indicated by one of the flags in Table 13-300. The following statements 
probe for the magnitude and direction of the electron current at a particular point.
PROBE X=0.25 Y=0.5 Z=0.3 J.ELEC V.MAG  NAME="Je magnitude (A/cm2)"
PROBE X=0.25 Y=0.5 Z=0.3 J.ELEC V.XANG NAME="Je angle in x-y plane"
PROBE X=0.25 Y=0.5 Z=0.3 J.ELEC V.ZANG NAME="Je angle from z axis"
Probing for Mobilities
Mobilities are direction-dependent functions, so when probing a mobility you must either 
indicate a direction or specify V.MAG, which in this case gives you the minimum over all 
directions at the specified point.
PROBE POS="(0.25,0.5,0.3)" N.MOB THETA=90 ZETA=60 NAME="Mu60"
PROBE POS="(0.25,0.5,0.3)" N.MOB V.X              NAME="MuX"
PROBE POS="(0.25,0.5,0.3)" N.MOB V.MAG            NAME="MuMin"
Integrating over a Polygonal Prism
The following command probes the total number of hydrogen atoms in a triangular prismatic 
region. The triangle is defined in the (z,x) plane, and the prism axis is in the y-direction.
PROBE INTEGRATED POLYGON="(0.0, 1.0) (1.0, 2.0) (2.0, 0.0)"
                 Y.MINIMUM=-0.5 Y.MAXIMUM=0.5
                 SPECIES="H" NAME="Total Hydrogen (atoms)"
Creating a Maximum Probe File
The following commands will create a comma separated value (CSV) file which contains a 
2D grid with the maximum value of a probed quantity in the specified direction. The 
MAX.FILE and NAME parameters must be specified. Localization parameters such as region,

Confidential
PROBE
Statements
material or X.MIN, X.MAX, Y.MIN, Y.MAX, Z.MIN, Z.MAX bounding box can also be 
specified along with the output grid parameters and probe direction.
probe 
name=pot1 
potential 
max.file 
dx.max.file=0.01 
dy.max.file=0.01 dz.max.file=0.01
After a LOAD or a SOLVE, a SAVE statement should be defined with the probe name and the 
file name:
save max.file=out.csv max.probe=pot1 dir.z.max.file
Adding a User Value
The following will add a quantity called 'hydrogen doping' to the log file and assign it to 
USER1.
PROBE name="hydrogen doping'  USER1
To set the USER1 quantity, use the MODELS statement. The following will set it to 1e15.
MODELS user1=1e15
Setting and varying the user parameters has NO EFFECT on the simulation, aside from 
adding a value to the log file. This is useful when (manually) varying quantities such as 
doping or various model parameters, to study their effect. This could be automated using the 
LOOP function in Deckbuild.

p_fae550a910.title: 13.34.3  Description
p_fae550a910.content:
13.34.3  Description
A PROBE statement must include a specification of either a point-location, a location type 
(MAX or MIN), or an accumulation function (AVERAGE or INTEGRATED), along with a 
specification of the particular quantity to be probed.
Table  13-294    Probe Location Parameters
Parameter
Effect
POSITION
Specifies the x, y, and z coordinates for a point probe.
X
Specifies the x coordinate for a point probe.
Y
Specifies the y coordinate for a point probe.
Z
Specifies the z coordinate for a point probe.
AVERAGE
The probed variable will be averaged over the specified locale.
INTEGRATED
The probed variable will be integrated over the specified locale. In Victory Device, 
only quantities defined on a per-volume basis can be integrated. These include carrier 
concentrations, thermal powers, and recombination/generation rates.
MAXIMUM
The probe will locate and use the maximum value of the probed variable.
MINIMUM
The probe will locate and use the minimum value of the probed variable.
A PROBE statement is the most accurate way to determine the value of many parameters 
calculated by Victory Device. Parameters stored on node points in the structure files for 
TonyPlot are often interpolated and subject to noise.

One of the scalars you can probe for is the component of the vector in a direction that you 
specify. The direction may be specified using either of two spherical coordinate systems. In 
the first, the parameter POLAR specifies the polar angle from the z-axis, while the parameter 
DIR specifies the angle around the z-axis in the x-y plane. The POLAR angle defaults to 90 
degrees, putting the direction in the x-y plane and making this system useful for probing both 
2D and 3D devices. In the second system, the parameter ZETA specifies the polar angle from 
the y-axis, while the parameter THETA specifies the angle around the y-axis in the x-z plane. 
This system is identical to that used to specify the orientation of the optical axis in hexagonal 
materials such as silicon carbide, except that on the PROBE statement, ZETA defaults to 90 
degrees. (See Hatakeyama’s Anisotropic Impact Ionization Model for 4H-SiC on page 306.) 
This second system is most likely to be useful for 3D devices composed of hexagonal 
materials. The parameters DIR and THETA both default to zero degrees, so that in either of

parameters are summarized in Table 13-299.

p_4466c951c7.title: 13.45  SPECIESCONTACT
p_4466c951c7.content:
13.45  SPECIESCONTACT
SPECIESCONTACT defines non-default boundary conditions for chemical species used in 
transport simulations. The default boundary condition is zero flux, which will be used for all 
boundaries and all species not covered by a SPECIESCONTACT statement.

p_0d5c795dd9.title: 13.45.1  Syntax
p_0d5c795dd9.content:
13.45.1  Syntax
SPECIESCONTACT extent SPECIES=species-name CONCENTRATION=value
              [VSURF=value] [BOUNDARY]
where the spatial extent of the species contact is
extent: electrode | (sc-id REGION=n | COORD.REGION=coord-string) | 
       (sc-name (box | cylinder))
The extent can be defined to be coincident with a previously defined electrode:
electrode: ELECTRODE.NAME=name | ELECTRODE.NUMBER=n | 
           ELECTRODE.SUBSTRATE
or, the species contact itself can be assigned a name or number and identified with a specified 
region, box, or cylinder:
sc-id: [NAME=name] [NUMBER=n]
box: [X.MINIMUM=value] [X.MAXIMUM=value] 
     [Y.MINIMUM=value] [Y.MAXIMUM=value] 
     [Z.MINIMUM=value] [Z.MAXIMUM=value]
cylinder: [R.MINIMUM=value] [R.MAXIMUM=value] 
          [A.MINIMUM=value] [A.MAXIMUM=value] 
          [Z.MINIMUM=value] [Z.MAXIMUM=value]
The SPECIESCONTACT statement also declares the concentration that the named species 
assumes at the boundary of the specified contact.

p_b23a5ee295.title: 13.45.2  Examples
p_b23a5ee295.content:
13.45.2  Examples
The following statements set the concentration of hydrogen to 2.01010 at the exterior 
boundaries of the source, drain, and gate electrodes:
SPECIESCONTACT ELECTRODE.NAME=source SPECIES="H" CONCENTRATION=2.0e10
SPECIESCONTACT ELECTRODE.NAME=drain  SPECIES="H" CONCENTRATION=2.0e10
SPECIESCONTACT ELECTRODE.NAME=gate   SPECIES="H" CONCENTRATION=2.0e10

p_92f73791ad.title: 13.45.3  Description
p_92f73791ad.content:
13.45.3  Description
A SPECIESCONTACT statement must do three things: identify the spatial region for which the 
species contact conditions apply, identify the species involved, and specify the boundary 
condition for the species. Boundary conditions may be set for different species in the same 
spatial region, but each separate species requires its own SPECIESCONTACT statement.
If the optional BOUNDARY flag is set, the boundary conditions will be imposed at all 
boundaries of the specified spatial region. Otherwise, boundary conditions are only imposed 
at the exterior boundaries (i.e. those bounding the exterior of the device).

Confidential
SPECIESCONTACT
Statements
The effect of each SPECIESCONTACT parameter is described in Table 13-353.
Table  13-353    Species Contact Parameters
Parameter
Effect
SPECIES
Identifies the species for which the boundary condition applies.
CONCENTRATION
Sets the concentration of the species at the boundary.
VSURF
Sets the surface velocity of the species at the boundary.
BOUNDARY
Causes the boundary condition to be applied at all boundaries of the specified 
spatial region.
ELECTRODE.NAME
Makes the species contact coincident with the named electrode.
ELECTRODE.NUMBER
Makes the species contact coincident with the numbered electrode.
ELECTRODE.SUBSTRATE
Makes the species contact coincident with the substrate electrode.
REGION
Makes the species contact coincident with the numbered region.
COORD.REGION
Makes the species contact coincident with the region containing the point 
specified by the supplied coord-string. This string consists of an ordered 
pair (in 2D) or triplet (in 3D) of real numbers that represent the 
x-, y-, and z-coordinates of the point, in units of m.
For example: COORD.REGION="(0.5,0.5,0.0)"
NAME
Names the species contact.
NUMBER
Numbers the species contact.
X.MAXIMUM
Specifies the maximum x-boundary for the species contact.
X.MINIMUM
Specifies the minimum x-boundary for the species contact.
Y.MAXIMUM
Specifies the maximum y-boundary for the species contact.
Y.MINIMUM
Specifies the minimum y-boundary for the species contact.

Context Title: Introduction & Document Info
Content: Importing a Structure File
Structure Definition
There are three methods in which to create device structures.
•
Importing them from another tool, such as DevEdit or Victory Process.
•
Loading a previously saved output file (structure file).
•
Defining them using Victory Device's internal commands.
This chapter will describe each of these, as well as how to save structure files for future use, 
or export to other tools.

Context Title: 2.1  Importing a Structure File
Content: 2.1  Importing a Structure File
Several Silvaco tools are able to create structure files, which can be imported to Victory Device
for simulation and analysis. These include process simulators (such as Victory Process), 
device editors (such as DevEdit and DevEdit 3D), and device simulators (such as Atlas,
Atlas3D, and Victory Device itself). Structure files may represent either two or three 
dimensional structures. Unlike other tools, Victory Device can handle both types and will 
automatically adapt.
The command to import a structure file is
MESH INFILE=filename.str
This will import the structure and any data (such as doping, material composition and stress) 
needed to run a simulation. It will not import actual simulation variables (such as potentials, 
and carrier concentrations). If you want to continue a simulation from a previously saved 
operating point, use the LOAD command (see Section 2.2 Loading a Previously Saved Output 
File).
When reading in a structure file, you may want to scale, stretch, or shift the structure. The 
options in Table 2-1 may be used on the MESH statement to accomplish this:
Table  2-1    Scale and Shift Options
Option
Description
SCALE=factor
Scales the structure evenly.
Stretch the structure in the x, y, or z direction.
SCALE.X=factor
SCALE.Y=factor
SCALE.Z=factor
Shift the structure by so many microns.
SHIFT.X=value
SHIFT.Y=value
SHIFT.Z=value
By default, all conductor (metal) regions defined on the grid will be treated as contacts, even 
if not specifically defined as such. You can prevent this by setting the CONDUCTOR flag on the 
MESH statement. Victory Device will then treat metal regions as non-electrode conductors, 
unless specifically defined otherwise. Alternatively, you can set the NO.CONTACT flag. This 
will load a structure entirely without electrodes, which you will then have to define explicitly 
using the ELECTRODE statement.

Context Title: 2.1  Importing a Structure File
Content: Confidential
Importing a Structure File
Structure Definition
When you import a structure file created by a process simulator, it may not contain any 
electrodes (contacts). These, however, are vital for device simulation.
You may add electrodes to the structure by using the ELECTRODE command.
For example
ELECTRODE NAME=gate MATERIAL=aluminum X.MIN=0.5 X.MAX=1.0 Y.MIN=0
defines an aluminum contact named 'gate' between 0.5 and 1.0 microns along the x axis 
and above 0 on the y axis. The box does not have to be specified completely, just the 
boundaries within the device. This will create a region named 'gate' and mark it as a 
contact.
ELECTRODE NAME=drain REGION=3
This defines region 3 to be a contact named 'drain'. Note that the structure file may already 
contain a region named drain (possibly even region 3), which may or may not be marked as a 
contact. This statement ensures that region 3  will definitely be treated as a 'drain' contact.
ELECTRODE NAME=SUBSTRATE BOTTOM
This defines an electrode named 'substrate' to be at the bottom of the device. In this case, 
'bottom' is not absolutely necessary, since 'substrate' implies a bottom contact by 
default.

Context Title: 2.1  Importing a Structure File
Content: Confidential
Loading a Previously Saved Output File
Structure Definition

Context Title: 2.2  Loading a Previously Saved Output File
Content: 2.2  Loading a Previously Saved Output File
Structure files saved by Victory Device (or Atlas) can be imported using the MESH command 
like all other structure files. When you do this, however, all of the device simulator specific 
data (such as potentials, electron concentrations, and temperature) will be lost. You will have 
to start your simulation at the very beginning with a SOLVE INIT, and then slowly ramp the 
boundary conditions to where you want them.
If you do want to continue a simulation from a previously saved operating point, use the LOAD
command:
LOAD INFILE=filename.str [CONTACT]
where filename.str is the previously saved output structure file. The CONTACT option tells 
Victory Device to load whatever contact structure was defined when the file was saved. This 
includes all workfunctions, and parasitic elements, as well as how the contacts were tied 
(slaved) together. Without this option all of these are reset, and you will have to re-define 
them.

Context Title: 2.2  Loading a Previously Saved Output File
Content: Confidential
Defining a Structure Using the Internal Commands
Structure Definition

Context Title: 2.3  Defining a Structure Using the Internal Commands
Content: 2.3  Defining a Structure Using the Internal Commands

Context Title: 2.3.1  Regular Cartesian Structure
Content: 2.3.1  Regular Cartesian Structure
To define a structure using the internal command language, you must first define a base mesh. 
This mesh or grid covers the physical simulation domain. The mesh is defined by a series of 
horizontal and vertical lines and the spacing between them. For example
X.MESH LOCATION= 0.0  SPACING=0.1
X.MESH LOCATION= 0.5  SPACING=0.01
X.MESH LOCATION= 1.0  SPACING=0.01
X.MESH LOCATION= 1.5  SPACING=0.1
Y.MESH LOCATION=-0.02 SPACING=0.01
Y.MESH LOCATION= 0.00 SPACING=0.001
Y.MESH LOCATION= 0.02 SPACING=0.001
Y.MESH LOCATION= 0.20 SPACING=0.05
Z.MESH LOCATION= 0.0  SPACING=0.2
Z.MESH LOCATION= 1.0  SPACING=0.2
This will create a base grid with an x spacing that smoothly varies from 0.1 micron to 0.01 
micron over the range from x=0.0 to x=0.5 microns, is constant at 0.01 micron between x=0.5 
and x=1.0 microns, and then gradually increases to 0.1 micron at x=1.5 microns. The y
spacing varies from 0.001 micron (between y=0.0 and y=0.02 microns) to 0.05 at the bottom 
of the device. The z spacing is a constant 0.2 micron for the entire width of the device.
Note:  In device simulation, the Y=0 is usually at the substrate or semiconductor surface, and 
the y coordinate indicates the distance into the semiconductor (i.e., down). So in this 
case, y=0.2 is the bottom of the device and y=-0.02 is the top.

Context Title: 2.3.2  Regions and Contacts
Content: 2.3.2  Regions and Contacts
You will now have to define the various regions, materials and contacts. For example
REGION NUMBER=1 MATERIAL=silicon
REGION NUMBER=2 MATERIAL=SiO2 y.max=0
This will first define the entire device to be made of silicon and then redefine anything above 
y=0 to be silicon dioxide. The same effect could be achieved with the statements:
REGION NUMBER=1 MATERIAL=silicon X.MIN=0 X.MAX=1.5 Y.MIN=0 Y.MAX=0.2
REGION NUMBER=2 MATERIAL=oxide   X.MIN=0 X.MAX=1.5 Y.MIN=-.02 Y.MAX=0
The first option is just simpler to write, easier to understand, and you will not have to change 
the box definitions if you wanted to alter the basic dimensions of the structure (e.g., define the 
z-grid to be from 0 to 5 micron). You must ensure that every element in the structure is 
defined to be in some region. If you leave a “empty” space somewhere, Victory Device will 
complain. If you want to define an “empty” space fill it with the material AIR.

Context Title: 2.3.2  Regions and Contacts
Content: Confidential
Defining a Structure Using the Internal Commands
Structure Definition
Next, define the contacts. For example:
ELECTRODE NAME=source MATERIAL=aluminum \
          X.MIN=0 X.MAX=0.5 Y.MIN=-0.01 Y.MAX=0
ELECTRODE NAME=drain  MATERIAL=aluminum \
          X.MIN=1 X.MAX=1.5 Y.MIN=-0.01 Y.MAX=0
ELECTRODE NAME=gate   MATERIAL=polysilicon \
          X.MIN=0.6 X.MAX=0.9 Y.MAX=-0.001
ELECTRODE NAME=substrate bottom
This will create two new aluminum contact regions named source and drain, as well as a 
polysilicon contact region named gate and a contact named substrate at the bottom of the 
device. If no material is specified, the contact will be a generic conductor.
Note that the bottom statement is not actually needed, because a substrate contact is assumed 
to be at the bottom by default.
The order of defining regions and electrodes is important, because later definitions will 
override the earlier ones. If, for example, you put the statement
REGION NUMBER=1 MATERIAL=silicon
after all other definitions, the entire device would be redefined as being silicon, regardless of 
what was set before.
If you do not want to use one of the predefined materials, you can specify a user-defined 
material by using the USER.MATERIAL parameter on the REGION and ELECTRODE statements 
(see section 2.9 User Defined Materials).

Context Title: 2.3.3  Voids
Content: 2.3.3  Voids
Normally you must define a region or electrode for every mesh point or element. If you leave 
a region undefined, Victory Device will exit with an error message. This prevents you from 
accidentally leaving undefined regions (voids), which can cause significant problems, 
especially when they are inside the device. Note that voids are not simulated and so leave a 
discontinuity in the solution.
If you want to include voids, there are two options:
•
Define region one as material AIR without specifying any boxes or spatial restrictions. 
This automatically sets any voids to be air (an insulator with a dielectric and optical index 
of one), and produces a valid solution in these regions. This is the preferred and 
physically more sensible solution.
•
Specify VOIDS on the mesh statement. This will exclude the non-defined regions from the 
simulation. Doing this will reduce the size of the simulation domain and possibly make 
the simulation slightly faster. However it will be less accurate and possibly will introduce 
discontinuities and errors into the solution, especially if the voids are inside the structure.
Care must be taken when using this option.

Context Title: 2.3.4  Automatic Meshing
Content: 2.3.4  Automatic Meshing
Rather than manually specifying the mesh lines and spacing, as explained in Section 2.3.1 
Regular Cartesian Structure, you can automatically generate the mesh lines based on the 
regions and electrodes you specify.

Context Title: 2.3.4  Automatic Meshing
Content: Confidential
Defining a Structure Using the Internal Commands
Structure Definition
To enable this feature, set the AUTO option on the MESH statement. This will automatically 
generate mesh lines on every region or electrode boundary you specify (for example, x.min, 
x.max, etc.).
If you want to generate extra lines in a particular region, you can specify the line spacing 
using the SX, SY, or SZ parameters, or you can set the number of lines you want to create in 
the region using the NX, NY or NZ parameters.
REGION NUM=1 MATERIAL=SILICON Y.MIN=1 Y.MAX=3 SY=0.1
This example creates a silicon region between Y=1 and Y=3 and as wide as the entire device 
(as required by other mesh, region, or electrode statements). The meshing algorithm 
automatically inserts lines at Y=1 and Y=3, and lines spaced 0.1 microns apart in between.
Alternatively you could specify:
REGION NUM=1 MATERIAL=SILICON Y.MIN=1 Y.MAX=3 NY=20
which would create the same region. Not specifying SY or NY would create no extra lines 
inside the region, but there would be lines at the region boundaries. The lines created by these 
statements are in addition to lines created elsewhere, such as on the mesh statements of other 
region statements.
Similarly you can include X.MIN, X.MAX, Z.MIN, Z.MAX, SX, NX, SZ, or NZ
parameters on a REGION statement. Similarly, lines will be generated at the outlines of any 
ELECTRODE you specify, although you cannot specify a line spacing on the ELECTRODE
statement.
Rather than specifying absolute positions on the REGION statement, you can specify the box 
boundaries relative to the TOP and BOTTOM of the device. For example
REGION num=2 MATERIAL=SIO2 TOP THICK=2 SY=0.2
would add a 2 micron thick layer of SiO2 on top of the device with a 0.2 micron line spacing. 
The TOP starts out at position 0 or whatever highest position was set on the Y.MESH
statement. The top position moves upwards as regions, electrodes, or Distributed Bragg 
Reflectors are specified. The regions do not have top be the full width of the device, you can 
limit the width by specifying:
REGION num=2 MATERIAL=SIO2 TOP THICK=2 SY=0.2 X.MIN=2 X.MAX=5
       NX=10
which would limit the region to between 2 and 5 microns in the X direction, and add an extra 
10 vertical lines through the region. If instead of going up from the top you want to go down, 
use the STAY option:
REGION num=3 MATERIAL=SIO2 TOP THICK=2 SY=0.2 STAY
This inserts a 2 micron thick region just below the top of the device which would not move.
Similarly, you can add layers to the bottom of the device using a statements like:
REGION num=4 MATERIAL=SILICON BOTTOM THICK=20 NY=10
This adds a 20 micron thick silicon layer to the bottom of the device, with 20 extra horizontal 
lines, and moves the location of the bottom down by 20 microns.

Context Title: 2.3.5  Distributed Bragg Reflectors (DBR)
Content: 2.3.5  Distributed Bragg Reflectors (DBR)
If you want to create a repeating stack of region layers, you can specify each layer as a 
separate region.
For a large number of layers, this could be tedious. Victory Device provides an easier method 
using the DBR (Distributed Bragg Reflector) statement. A DBR consists of a repeating 
sequence to two alternating regions with different material properties (materials, 
compositions, doping, optical index, etc.).
The MAT1 and MAT2 parameters specify the material names of the two materials. Note that 
MAT1 and MAT2 can be specified as the same material (with different x-compositions or 
dopings, for example).
The X1.COMP, Y1.COMP, X2.COMP, and Y2.COMP parameters are used to specify the X 
and Y composition fractions of the two materials for ternary and quaternary materials.
The thicknesses (in microns) of the two layers are specified by the THICK1 and THICK2
parameters. The doping of the two layers is specified using NA1 and NA2 for acceptors, and 
ND1 and ND2 for donors.
The spacing in the two regions can be specified using the SPA1 and SPA2 parameters, which 
work like the SY parameter on the REGION statement. Alternatively you can use the N1 and 
N2 parameters to specify the number of grid lines inside the layers.
The HALF.CYCLE parameter specifies the total number of layers. An odd values specifies that 
one more layer of MAT1 is to be used than of MAT2.
The TOP and BOTTOM parameters of the DBR statement are used just like the REGION
statement, except that the first material to be added to the top/bottom of the device is always 
of MAT1.
To create a structure with seven alternating silicon and germanium layers, as shown in Figure 
2-1, specify
DBR BOTTOM THICK1=0.1 THICK2=0.2 HALF.CYCLES=7 MAT1=silicon
    MAT2=germanium N1=6 N2=9 ND1=1e16 ND2=2e16

and composition from the values in layer 1 to those in layer 2 (assuming the materials in the

and TH21 (going from region 1 to region 2 and region 2 to region 1, respectively). You can

Context Title: 2.3.6  Doping
Content: 2.3.6  Doping
Finally you may define the doping for the device. For example:
DOPING REGION=1 UNIFORM P.TYPE CONC=1e17
DOPING REGION=1 UNIFORM N.TYPE CONC=1e19 X.MAX=0.62 Y.MAX=0.02 
DOPING REGION=1 UNIFORM N.TYPE CONC=1e19 X.MIN=0.88 Y.MAX=0.02
will define a background p-type doping of 1.0e17 and two n-type regions, with a doping of 
1.0e19. The doping will only affect region 1 (i.e., the silicon region).
By default, doping is cumulative. Thus, the n-type doping in this example will be in addition 
to the previously set p-type (or any other) doping. However, Victory Device offers you a 
choice in how the profile specified on a DOPING statement is combined with a previously-
specified doping profile. There are four possible modes: APPEND, MAXIMUM, MINIMUM, and 
REPLACE. These are described in Table 13-48 in Section 13.7 DOPING.
For UNIFORM doping, the doping profile drops to zero right outside the box. It you want a
more gradual roll-off, there are several possibilities. The first is to use a Gaussian roll-off 
profile. This is done by setting GAUSSIAN (instead of UNIFORM) and specifying a 
CHARACTERISTIC length, which is the standard deviation (in microns) for the roll-off.
DOPING N.TYPE GAUSSIAN CONC=1e19 CHARACTERISTIC=0.01 X.MAX=0.62
       Y.MAX=0.02
This adds an n-type doping inside the box x<0.62 and y<0.02, and a Gaussian roll-off with a 
standard deviation of 0.01 microns in all directions outside the box. You may also set 
different standard deviations in various directions using 
X.CHARACTERISTIC, 
Y.CHARACTERISTIC, or Z.CHARACTERISTIC. Instead of a Gaussian profile you may also 
use a complementary error function profile by using ERFC instead of GAUSSIAN.

Context Title: 2.3.6  Doping
Content: Confidential
Defining a Structure Using the Internal Commands
Structure Definition
Another possibility is to import a tabular doping profile. To do this specify
DOPING P.TYPE INFILE=<filename> ASCII BACKDOPE=1e15 
       DIRECTION=X START=2
This will import a tabular doping profile from an ASCII file named <filename>, which needs 
to be of the format:
<depth in microns>  <doping in cm-3>
    <depth in microns>  <doping in cm-3>
    <depth in microns>  <doping in cm-3>
The profile will be applied in the x direction (downward direction by default), starting at x=2 
micron and going to the last depth specified in the file. Beyond the last point, the doping will 
be set either to the specified background doping (1.0e15 in this case), or by default to the last 
doping specified in the file.
In addition to this, you may import a doping profiles directly from a file created by Silvaco 
tools like ATHENA or Victory Process. For a 1D profile the procedure is similar using and 
ASCII file. Just specify MASTER instead of ASCII (for files in Silvaco master format).
IF the Silvaco file you want to import is not a 1D profile, but a full structure file (in 2D or 
3D), specify
DOPING N.TYPE INFILE=<filename> MASTER X.MAX=0.62 
         Y.MAX=0.02 C.MULT=2
This will import whatever n.type doping exists in the structure file within the specified box, 
and multiply it by a factor of 2 in this example. If no box is specified, the doping will be 
imported for the entire device. You do have to specify what type of doping (n.type, p.type, or 
a specific species) you want to import. The C.MULT is optional.

2.3.6 Doping) is shown in Figure 2-3.

Context Title: 2.3.7  Specific Doping Components
Content: 2.3.7  Specific Doping Components
A Victory Process structure file may include some specific doping elements such as 
Phosphorous or Boron. These are read in by Victory Device and are aggregated as either 
donors or acceptors depending on the particular chemical type. If both the Active and 
Chemical fields of any particular type are present, the Active field is used preferentially. It is 
also possible to specify a particular doping element on the DOPING statement in a Victory 
Device deck. The donor dopants which can be specified are PHOSPHORUS, ARSENIC, 
ANTIMONY (for Si, Ge) and NITROGEN (for SiC). The acceptor dopants which can be 
specified are BORON, ALUMINUM and INDIUM. Each dopant can have its own spatial 
distribution. The donors are aggregated into the donor doping concentration for the device, 
and the acceptors are aggregated into the acceptor doping concentration. The individual 
doping elements may be visualized in any Standard Structure File (SSF) output using the 
SAVE statement.

Context Title: 3.1  Basic Semiconductor Equations
Content: 3.1  Basic Semiconductor Equations
This chapter describes the mathematical equations and physical models that are implemented 
in Victory Device. The basic equations, derived from Maxwell’s laws, link together the 
electrostatic potential and the carrier densities. These equations are supplemented by 
mathematical models for various physical processes. A general purpose device simulator, 
such as Victory Device, solves these equations within some simulation domain. The thirty 
years since this approach was first introduced [165,189] have demonstrated its general 
applicability to semiconductor devices.
The basic semiconductor equations include:
•
Poisson’s Equation (see Section Poisson’s Equation), 
•
Continuity equations (see Section Carrier Continuity Equations), and 
•
Transport equations for carrier momentum and possibly carrier energy (see Sections 3.1.3 
Transport Equations, 3.2 The Drift-Diffusion Transport Model, 3.3 The Energy Balance 
Transport Model, and 3.4 The Boltzmann Transport Equation Solver).
Supplemental equations include:
•
The lattice heat flow equation (see Section The Lattice Heat Flow Equation).
Poisson’s Equation relates variations in the electrostatic potential to local charge densities. 
The continuity and transport equations describe the way that the electron and hole densities 
evolve as a result of transport processes, generation processes, and recombination processes. 
And the lattice heat flow equation accounts for lattice temperature variations and the thermal 
environment.

Context Title: 3.1.3  Transport Equations
Content: 3.1.3  Transport Equations
The current density equations, or charge transport models, are usually obtained by applying 
approximations and simplifications to the Boltzmann Transport Equation. These assumptions 
can result in a number of different transport models such as the drift-diffusion model, the 
energy balance model, or the hydrodynamic model. The choice of the charge transport model 
subsequently exerts a major influence on the choice of generation and recombination models 
and the choice of mobility models.
The simplest useful model of charge transport is the drift-diffusion model. This model has the 
attractive feature that it does not introduce any independent variables in addition to 
, and 
. Until recently, the drift-diffusion model was adequate for nearly all devices that were 
technologically feasible. The drift-diffusion approximation, however, becomes less accurate 
for smaller feature sizes. More advanced energy balance and hydrodynamic models are 
therefore becoming popular for simulating deep submicron devices. Victory Device uses the 
drift-diffusion model by default, but the advanced models are available if you need them. (See 
Sections 3.2 The Drift-Diffusion Transport Model, 3.3 The Energy Balance Transport Model, 
and 3.4 The Boltzmann Transport Equation Solver)

n
p
The charge transport models and the models for generation and recombination in Victory 
Device make use of some concepts associated with carrier statistics. These concepts are 
summarized in Section Theory of Carrier Statistics.

Context Title: 3.1.4  The Lattice Heat Flow Equation
Content: 3.1.4  The Lattice Heat Flow Equation
In general, the generation and recombination rates may depend on the temperature of the 
semiconductor lattice. Certain parameters in the transport equations are likewise temperature-
dependent. Conversely, generation, recombination, and resistive effects may all contribute to 
the heating or cooling of the lattice. When these effects are important, the lattice heat flow 
equation must be solved in conjunction with the Poisson, continuity, and transport equations. 
Victory Device will solve the lattice heat flow equation when the LAT.TEMP flag is set on a 
MODELS statement.

electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection devices. And a self-consistent accounting of lattice

Content: 3.1.6  The Conductor Current Equation

they have been specifically defined as such. If you want to simulate current flow in these

not contacts. It will do the same for any given metal if you set the RESISTIVE flag on an 
appropriate MATERIAL statement. This might be useful if you wanted to simulate power 
devices, fuses, or large power supply buses.

semiconductors) there is no  recombination/generation, and the current continuity equations

The previous subsections show how to set the quasi-Fermi levels for the entire device or for 
individual regions. You can also set the quasi-Fermi levels just for doping wells, that is to say 
areas of contiguous doping of one type or another. To do this you specify any point within the 
region using the position speciﬁer syntax donor.well.m = ’x,y,z’ for donors and 
acceptor.well.m = ’x,y,z’ for acceptors. These are specified on the MODELS
statement. The ordinal m can be any integer between 1 and 9, meaning that up to nine 
separate donor wells and nine separate acceptor wells can be modified in a single device. The

In order to set the quasi-Fermi level for a doping well region you use the syntax dwnb(m) for 
donor wells or dwpb(m) for acceptor wells. These are specified on the SOLVE statement, and

allows precise specification of quasi-Fermi level for zero-carrier and one-carrier solutions. 
Note also that any wells which cross region boundaries will need a separate position speciﬁer 
for each region in which they occur.

Context Title: 3.3   The Energy Balance Transport Model
Content: 3.3   The Energy Balance Transport Model
Like the drift-diffusion model, the energy balance transport model is derived by taking 
moments of the Boltzmann Transport Equation. Besides balance equations for the carrier 
density and momentum, the energy balance model includes balance equations for the carrier 
energy and energy flux [128]. In Victory Device, the energy balance model is based on the 
derivation by Stratton [204,205].
By applying certain assumptions, the energy balance model decomposes into the 
hydrodynamic model [22,23,140]. Collectively, models like these are known as hot carrier 
transport models.
Hot carrier transport models are capable of modeling non-local transport effects that can have 
a significant influence on the terminal properties of submicron devices. These phenomena 
include velocity overshoot, diffusion associated with the carrier temperatures, and the 
dependence of impact ionization rates on carrier energy distributions.
Setting the HCTE flag on a MODELS statement activates the energy balance equations 
describing hot carrier transport. Alternatively, setting HCTE.EL on a MODELS statement 
activates the equations for electrons, while setting HCTE.HO activates the equations for holes.

Context Title: 4.1  Overview
Content: 4.1  Overview
This chapter describes the facilities that Victory Device has for modeling the transport and 
reaction of chemical species within the body of a semiconductor device. These facilities may 
be used for studies of performance degradation, for simulation of complex charge-capture 
mechanisms, and for the simulation of charge-transport by atomic species, as well as for 
investigating the behavior of novel devices[221]. Victory Device is able to simulate the 
transport and reaction of an arbitrary number of chemical species, limited only by time 
constraints and the availability of memory in your computer.
Individual species may be mobile or fixed. As the name suggests, mobile species—which 
may also be described as transportable or diffusing species—can move around within the 
device. In contrast, fixed species remain at their original location. Fixed species participating 
in chemical reactions represent trap states, so these species may also be called trapping 
species. A closed set of trapping species participating in chemical reactions with each other 
constitute a multi-state trap.
The specific topics covered in this chapter include:
•
Equations for the conservation and transport of chemical species, along with an 
accounting of the effect that charged species (ions) have on the charge-state of the device. 
These are discussed in Section 4.2 Chemical Species Equations for Semiconductor 
Devices.
•
Definition of the composition and charge of a chemical species. This is discussed in 
Section 4.3 Chemical Species Definition.
•
The initial distribution of chemical species within the device. This is discussed in Section 
4.4 Initialization of Species Concentrations.
•
Specification of transport properties and related models, which typically depend on both 
the species in question and on the material through which it is being transported. These 
are discussed in Section 4.5 Properties of Chemical Species in Materials.
•
Facilities for the definition of chemical reactions, as well as the generation and 
recombination interactions between species, electrons, and holes. These are discussed in 
Section 4.6 Chemical Reactions.
•
Interface models for species. These are discussed in Section 4.7 Interface Conditions for 
Chemical Species.
•
Boundary conditions for the species continuity equation. These are discussed in Section 
4.8 Boundary Conditions for Chemical Species.
•
Simulations using frozen, equilibrium, or transient chemistry. These are discussed in 
Section 4.9 Chemistry Simulation Types.
•
How to save chemical species data to structure and log files. This is discussed in Section 
4.10 Output of Chemical Species Data.
•
The concepts presented in this chapter are tied together in Section 4.11 Examples.
Generic Ion Transport and Generic Ion Reactions
The most general and flexible way to set up solid-state chemistry simulations in Victory 
Device is to use named species with specified chemical formulas. However, you can also use 
the syntax for unnamed generic species that is supported by Atlas[195] in its Generic Ion 
Transport, Generic Ion Reaction, and Multi-State Trap models. Both methods are discussed in 
the sections that follow.

Context Title: 4.2  Chemical Species Equations for Semiconductor Devices
Content: 4.2  Chemical Species Equations for Semiconductor Devices
For semiconductor devices, the basic chemical species equations include:
•
The continuity equation for species conservation (see Section 4.2.1);
•
The flux equation describing species transport (see Section 4.2.2).
Also, some existing equations are modified by the addition of species terms:
•
The Poisson Equation for the electrostatic potential is modified by additional terms in the 
expression for the space charge density (see Section 4.2.3 Modification of the Space 
Charge Density and Section 3.1.1 Poisson’s Equation);
•
The electron and hole continuity equations are modified by additional recombination and 
generation terms that arise from chemical reactions (see Section 4.6 Chemical Reactions).
•
The heat generation rate in the lattice heat flow equation is modified by the heat released 
or absorbed by chemical reactions (see Section 4.6.6 Heat Generation from Reactions and 
Section 3.12.3 Heat Generation).

Context Title: 4.3  Chemical Species Definition
Content: 4.3  Chemical Species Definition
There are two ways to define chemical species in Victory Device. The most general and 
flexible way is to define a named species, with a specified chemical formula. You can define 
as many uniquely-named species as you like. Alternatively, you can define up to three generic 
species (also known as generic ions). Named species are preferred

Context Title: 4.3.1  Named Species Definition
Content: 4.3.1  Named Species Definition
In Victory Device, the easiest way to define a chemical species is by means of the SPECIES
statement. This allows you to specify the chemical formula and charge of the species, as well 
as to give it a distinct name. The formula and charge are required elements of the definition, 
but the name is optional. If a name is not supplied, one will be generated from the formula 
and charge, but it’s often more straightforward to just name the species yourself.
Species Formulas
The formula is specified as a string of elemental components, with the components separated 
by a period ‘.’ or colon ‘:’. Each component must begin with a standard elemental symbol, 
optionally followed by an integer indicating the multiplicity of that element. The species 
charge is specified as a signed integer. Positive integers denote positive charges and negative 
integers denote negative charges, as you would expect.
For example, a presumably interfacial silicon atom passivated by a hydrogen atom could be 
specified by the statement
SPECIES FORMULA="Si:H" CHARGE=0
A molecule of diatomic hydrogen would be specified by
SPECIES FORMULA="H2" CHARGE=0
while a proton would be specified by
SPECIES FORMULA="H" CHARGE=1
Within the FORMULA, the symbols for the individual elements may appear in any order, but 
each element may appear no more than once.
Species Names
Victory Device identifies chemical species by their names, so all species must be named by 
some means. Species defined by a SPECIES statement may be named explicitly by means of 
the NAME parameter, but if a name is not supplied, one will be generated from the chemical 
formula and charge. Generic species (see Section 4.3.2 Generic Species Definition) are 
named automatically as “Species1”, “Species2”, and “Species3”. Also, “e-” is reserved as the 
species name for electrons, and “h+” is reserved as the species name for holes.
On the SPECIES statement, the optional name string may include any keyboard character 
except a space, but it must not start with a numeral. The string must be quoted if it includes 
any non-alphanumeric characters. Case is significant in species names.
For example, the following statements will define two species, respectively named “H+” and 
“Hydrogen”:
SPECIES FORMULA="H" CHARGE=1
SPECIES FORMULA="H" CHARGE=0 NAME="Hydrogen"

Content: Confidential

Note:  The SPECIES FORMULA only identifies the chemical composition of a species. It says 
nothing about the chemical structure. Consequently, if you have two species that have 
the same chemical composition but different structures, you should be sure to give them
 
distinct names.

Context Title: 4.3.2  Generic Species Definition
Content: 4.3.2  Generic Species Definition
In Victory Device you may use a MODELS statement to define up to three generic species (also 
known as generic ions). This facility is provided for backward compatibility with Atlas[195].
You declare the number of generic species to simulate by means of the NSPECIES parameter. 
Setting MODELS NSPECIES=1 enables the simulation of “Species1”, setting NSPECIES=2
enables the simulation of “Species1” and “Species2”, and setting NSPECIES=3 enables the 
simulation of “Species1”, “Species2”, and “Species3”. These species names are generated 
automatically.
You set the composition number (or elemental multiplicity) for “Species1” by specifying an 
integer value for SPECIES1.A. “Species2” and “Species3” are handled similarly. In contrast 
to Atlas, Victory Device will not attempt to work out the composition numbers automatically 
from REACTION statements. Consequently, you must specify the composition number for 
each generic species you are simulating.
Likewise, you set the charge on “Species1” by specifying a signed integer value for 
SPECIES1.Z. Again, “Species2” and “Species3” are handled in the same way. Just as with 
named (non-generic) species, positive integers denote positive charges and negative integers 
denote negative charges.
For example, the following statement defines two generic species, respectively named 
“Species1” and “Species2”:
MODELS NSPECIES=2 SPECIES1.A=1 SPECIES1.Z=1 \
                  SPECIES2.A=1 SPECIES2.Z=0
The first of these has a positive unit charge, while the second species is neutral. Both species 
consist of a single atom of a generic element “X”.

Context Title: 4.4  Initialization of Species Concentrations
Content: 4.4  Initialization of Species Concentrations
Species concentrations must be initialized prior to the start of a simulation. There are several 
ways to do this in Victory Device, depending on whether you want specify species doping in 
bulk regions, along interfaces, or using data from a structure file.

Context Title: 4.4.1  Bulk Doping
Content: 4.4.1  Bulk Doping
Species concentrations in bulk regions may be initialized by means of DOPING statements. 
For example:
SPECIES FORMULA="H" CHARGE=0 NAME="H"
DOPING REGION=1 SPECIES.NAME="H" UNIFORM CONCENTRATION=1e19
DOPING REGION=2 SPECIES.NAME="H" UNIFORM CONCENTRATION=2e18
DOPING REGION=3 SPECIES.NAME="H" UNIFORM CONCENTRATION=3e17
DOPING REGION=4 SPECIES.NAME="H" UNIFORM CONCENTRATION=4e16
will initialize the concentrations of hydrogen in several regions of a device. The 
concentrations here are given per unit (cm3) of volume.
By default, doping operations for a given species in a given region are cumulative. However, 
Victory Device offers you a choice in how the profile specified on a DOPING statement is 
combined with a previously-specified doping profile. There are four possible modes: 
APPEND, MAXIMUM, MINIMUM, and REPLACE. These are described in Table 13-48. See 
Section 13.7 DOPING for details on these, as well as on the other flags and parameters that 
control doping.

Context Title: 4.4.2  Interfacial Doping
Content: 4.4.2  Interfacial Doping
Species concentrations along interfaces may be initialized by means of INTERFACE
statements. For example:
SPECIES FORMULA="Si"   CHARGE=0  NAME="Si"
SPECIES FORMULA="Si:H" CHARGE=0  NAME="SiH"
SPECIES FORMULA="Si:H" CHARGE=-1 NAME="SiH-"
INTERFACE S.I SPECIES.NAME="Si"   CONCENTRATION=5e11
INTERFACE S.I SPECIES.NAME="SiH"  CONCENTRATION=3e11
INTERFACE S.I SPECIES.NAME="SiH-" CONCENTRATION=2e11
will initialize the concentration of three species along semiconductor/insulator interfaces. The 
concentrations here are given per unit (cm2) of interfacial area.
Along semiconductor/insulator (S.I), semiconductor/conductor (S.C), and semiconductor/
metal (S.M) interfaces, species doping specified on an INTERFACE statement will be placed 
entirely on the semiconductor side. Along semiconductor/semiconductor (S.S) and insulator/
insulator (I.I) interfaces, the doping will be split equally on both sides. For other flags and 
parameters controlling placement, see Section 13.15 INTERFACE.

Context Title: 4.4.3  Initialization from a Structure File
Content: 4.4.3  Initialization from a Structure File
There are several ways to initialize species concentrations from a structure file:
1.
You can create species doping as described above, and then save the results to a structure 
file. If you then load that structure file using a MESH statement, Victory Device will read 
in the saved doping and use it to initialize the species concentrations.
2.
You can save the results of a simulation to a structure file. If you then load that structure 
file using a LOAD statement, Victory Device will read the saved species concentrations 
and start with those.
3.
You can use the F.DOPING parameter on a DOPING statement to identify a C-Interpreter
file that initializes species doping based on supplemental C-Interpreter inputs 
corresponding to structure-file data (such as the Active hydrogen doping concentration), 
See Section A.4 Supplemental Inputs to C-Interpreter Functions.

Context Title: 4.5.3  Maximum Species Concentration (Solubility Limit)
Content: 4.5.3  Maximum Species Concentration (Solubility Limit)
Sometimes, there is a physical limit to the concentration of a species within a material. For 
example: the species may be confined to particular sites interstitial to the crystal structure, in 
which case the concentration is limited by the spatial density of those sites. In Victory Device, 
you can handle such cases by specifying a limiting maximum value for the species 
concentration.
Specification of a Concentration Limit for Named Species
To specify the maximum concentration for a named species, you begin the MATERIAL
statement with a SPECIES.NAME parameter identifying the species in question. The species 
must have been previously defined on a SPECIES statement. You then specify the 
concentration limit by specifying a value for the SPECIES.MAXIMUM.CONCENTRATION. For 
example:
MATERIAL MATERIAL="Silicon" SPECIES.NAME="H" \
                            SPECIES.MAXIMUM.CONCENTRATION=1.0e21
Specification of a Concentration Limit for Generic Species
When specifying material-dependent diffusivities for generic species, the SPECIES.NAME
parameter is not used. Instead, there are species-specific parameters. For example, to specify 
a concentration limit for “Species1”, you might have
MATERIAL SPECIES1.MAXIMUM.CONCENTRATION=1.0e21.
Concentration limits for “Species2” and “Species3” may be specified similarly.

Context Title: 4.6.1  Reaction Formulas for Named Species
Content: 4.6.1  Reaction Formulas for Named Species
Specifying the formula for a reaction between named species is very easy: you simply write 
the formula using the ordinary notation for chemical reactions and assign it (as a string) to the 
FORMULA parameter on a REACTION statement. For example:
SPECIES FORMULA="H2"   CHARGE=0 NAME="Hydrogen"
SPECIES FORMULA="O2"   CHARGE=0 NAME="Oxygen"
SPECIES FORMULA="H2:0" CHARGE=0 NAME="Water"
REACTION FORMULA="2Hydrogen + Oxygen <=> 2Water"
There are several important things to note about the syntax of reaction formulas:
•
The REACTION formula uses species names, not species formulas.
•
Each species name may be preceded by an optional number, giving the multiplicity.
•
Spaces in the formula are significant. They separate each component from the next, and 
must be present.
•
The reactants (on the left side of the formula) must be separated from the products (on the 
right side) by the special symbol "<=>".
•
Each species name may appear at most once on each side of the reaction.
•
The reaction formula must be chemically balanced. If Victory Device encounters an 
unbalanced reaction formula, it will exit with an error message to that effect.
Here is a more realistic example for device simulation, defining ionization and dimerization 
reactions for hydrogen:
SPECIES FORMULA="H2" CHARGE=0 NAME="H2"
SPECIES FORMULA="H"  CHARGE=0 NAME="H"
SPECIES FORMULA="H"  CHARGE=1 NAME="H+"
REACTION FORMULA="2H <=> H2"
REACTION FORMULA="H  + h+ <=> H+"
REACTION FORMULA="H+ + e- <=> H"
As noted in Section 4.3.1 Named Species Definition, “e-” is reserved as the species name for 
electrons, and “h+” is reserved as the species name for holes.
In addition to specifying the reaction formula, a REACTION statement must also specify the 
reaction rates, as described in Section 4.6.3 Reaction Rates.

Context Title: 4.6.2  Reaction Formulas for Generic Species
Content: 4.6.2  Reaction Formulas for Generic Species
To specify reaction formulas for generic species, you could use the system for named species 
described above, using the reserved generic species names “Species1”, “Species2”, and 
“Species3”, along with “e-” and “h+” if the reaction involves electrons or holes. 
Alternatively, you can use the legacy syntax that is used by Atlas[195], specifying the species 
multiplicities “before” and “after” the reaction. Using the legacy syntax, the ionization and 
dimerization reactions for hydrogen may be described as
MODELS SPECIES1.A=2 SPECIES1.Z=0 \
       SPECIES2.A=1 SPECIES2.Z=0 \
       SPECIES3.A=1 SPECIES3.Z=1
REACTION BEFORE.SP2=2 AFTER.SP1=1
REACTION BEFORE.SP2=1 BEFORE.P=1 AFTER.SP3=1
REACTION BEFORE.SP3=1 BEFORE.N=1 AFTER.SP2=1
These reactions are completely equivalent to those at the end of Section 4.6.1 Reaction 
Formulas for Named Species, although you will probably find the new syntax to be clearer.
Once again, in addition to specifying the reaction formula, a REACTION statement must also 
specify the reaction rates, as described in Section 4.6.3 Reaction Rates.

Context Title: 4.6.7  .Multi-State Traps
Content: 4.6.7  .Multi-State Traps
In general, traps are sites within a crystal lattice where a chemical reaction takes place 
between an immobile (or trapping) chemical species and a mobile (or trapped) chemical 
species or charge carrier. These chemical reactions transform one trapping species into 
another, which can also be regarded as changing the state of the trap. Each trap state, then, 
corresponds to a unique immobile species.
Two-state traps where the trapped species is an electron or a hole are discussed in Section 
3.9.4 Traps and Defects. Traps with more than two states are discussed in this section, as are 
two-state traps where the trapped species is not an electron or hole.
Multi-State Traps for Generic Species
For generic species, Victory Device supports the multi-state trap model used by Atlas[195]. 
This model is framed in terms of the occupation probabilities of the trap states. The time 
evolution of each occupation probability is governed by the transition rates between the 
different states, with these transition rates being given by a C-Interpreter function.
In this model, a trap can have from two to five trapping states. For a trap with

To enable this model for bulk traps, you specify the MSCTRAP flag on a TRAP statement. To 
enable it for interface traps, you specify the MSCTRAP flag on an INTTRAP statement. In either 
case, you must also use the MSC.NSTATES parameter to specify the number of trapping states. 
As mentioned, this can be any value from 2 to 5.
Each trapping state consists of a base state combined with 0 to 5 trapped species chosen from 
the list “e-”, “h+”, “Species1”, “Species2”, and “Species3”. You define a trap state by 
specifying the multiplicity of each trapped species present, along with the charge held by the 
state. For State 1, for example, you would set these multiplicities using the MSC1.ELEC, 
MSC1.HOLE, MSC1.SP1, MSC1.SP2, and MSC1.SP3 parameters. The default multiplicity is 
0, so you don’t have to specify parameters for species that are not present. States 2 through 5 
are defined similarly.
You may also specify a charge for each trapping state. For State 1, the charge is specified by 
the MSC1.CHARGE parameter, and the charges for States 2 through 5 are specified similarly. If 
you do not specify a charge, Victory Device will infer it from the charges of the trapped 
species present. If you do specify a charge, Victory Device may adjust the multiplicity of 
electrons or holes to make the state definition consistent.
For each of the 
 states of the trap, you must specify the initial occupation probability. These 
are set by the parameters MSC1.FT0, MSC2.FT0, etc. As required by Equation 4-43, the 
initial occupation probabilities must sum to 1.0. Victory Device will check this and will issue 
an error message if the condition is not met.
N
In this model, you must also specify whether each trap state is defined with respect to the 
conduction band or the valence band, and you may optionally specify an offset from that 
band. For example, setting MSC1.ET.CB and MSC1.ELEVEL=0.1 would specify that State 1 
of the trap has an energy level offset 0.1 eV from the conduction band. The trap-state energies 
are passed to the C-Interpreter function that calculates the inter-state transition rates.
To complete the specification of a multi-state trap, you must specify the trap DENSITY and 
supply a C-Interpreter function to calculate the transition rates. The C-Interpreter function is 
called msctransitionrates and the prototype is given in the file template.lib. You use the 
F.MSCRATES parameter to specify the name of the file containing your version. The function 
allows you to return derivatives of the rate with respect to the dependent variables, and you 
should do this for optimum performance.
Among the input parameters to msctransitionrates are two integers, i and j, which are 
never simultaneously the same. Both run from 1 up to the number of trapping states. These 
allow a transition rate 
 to be programmed for each combination of starting-state i and
aij
ending state j. Figure 4-2 illustrates the transition rates for a three-state trap.

As mentioned previously, Victory Device identifies chemical species by their names, so all 
species must be named by some means. For multi-state traps, Victory Device will 
automatically generate species names for the trap states. These names follow a pattern 
indicating whether the trap is a bulk trap (Bt) or an interface trap (It), the trap number, and the 
state number. For example, State 1 of the 1st multi-state bulk trap would be named 
“Bt[1]State[1].” Likewise, State 4 of the 3rd multi-state interface trap would be named 
“It[3]State[4].” The trap number is present in the name because Victory Device allows you to 
define an arbitrary number of multi-state traps.
From the compositions of the different trap states, Victory Device deduces the chemical 
reactions that transform one state to another. Together with the rates provided by 
msctransitionrates, these reactions are used to calculate the net generation rate for each 
participating mobile species (including electrons and holes), according to Equation 4-39. If 
you set MODELS PRINT, Victory Device will print the reaction formulas to the run-time 
output.
Multi-State Traps for Named Species
For named species, there is no special syntax for specifying multi-state traps, because none is 
required. You simply set up the species and reactions in the normal way, as described in 
Section 4.3.1 Named Species Definition, Section 4.4 Initialization of Species Concentrations, 
and Section 4.6.1 Reaction Formulas for Named Species. Instead of using a C-Interpreter file, 
reaction rates are specified as described in Section 4.6.3 Reaction Rates. Victory Device
automatically identifies any species with zero diffusivity as an immobile trapping species. A 
multi-state trap is constituted from the combination of trapping species that participate in a 
closed set of trapping reactions.
Examples of Multi-State Traps
Here is an example of a multi-state trap for generic species, set up to simulate the degradation 
of a passivated interface:
# Define 1 mobile species, representing a hydrogen atom
MODELS NSPECIES=1 SPECIES1.Z=0
# Diffusivity properties for hydrogen
MATERIAL SPECIES1.EA=0.15 SPECIES1.AF=0.15 SPECIES1.HOP=8e-7
# Define the 3 trapping states, total density, and initial fractions
# State transition rates are defined in "h_trans.c"
INTTRAP S.I DENSITY=1E12 \
    MSCTRAP MSC.NSTATES=3 F.MSCRATES="h_trans.c" 
    MSC1.FT0=0.5 MSC1.SP1=0              MSC1.CHARGE=0  MSC1.ET.CB \
    MSC2.FT0=0.2 MSC2.SP1=1 MSC2.ELEC=-1 MSC2.CHARGE=-1 MSC2.ET.CB \
    MSC3.FT0=0.3 MSC3.SP1=1              MSC3.CHARGE=0  MSC3.ET.VB

Here is the same example, set up using named species. Assuming that the C-Interpreter 
function in "h_trans.c" calculates transition rates corresponding to the reaction rates given 
below, these two examples are completely equivalent.
# Define 1 mobile species, representing a hydrogen atom
SPECIES FORMULA="H"    CHARGE=0  NAME="H"
# Define the 3 trapping species
SPECIES FORMULA="Si"   CHARGE=0  NAME="Si"
SPECIES FORMULA="Si:H" CHARGE=-1 NAME="SiH-"
SPECIES FORMULA="Si:H" CHARGE=0  NAME="SiH"
# Initialize the trapping species concentrations
INTERFACE S.I SPECIES.NAME="Si"   CONCENTRATION=0.5e12
INTERFACE S.I SPECIES.NAME="SiH-" CONCENTRATION=0.2e12
INTERFACE S.I SPECIES.NAME="SiH"  CONCENTRATION=0.3e12
# Diffusivity properties for hydrogen
MATERIAL SPECIES.NAME="H" \
         SPECIES.EA=0.15 SPECIES.AF=0.15 SPECIES.HOP=8e-7
# Define the trapping reactions and reaction rates
REACTION FORMULA="Si  + H  <=> SiH"  FOR.RATE=1.0e-15 FOR.EA=0.0 \
REACTION FORMULA="SiH + e- <=> SiH-" FOR.RATE=1.1e-7  FOR.EA=0.0 \
                                     REV.RATE=1.1e-12 REV.EA=0.8
Note:  These two examples are intended to illustrate the syntax for multi-state traps. The
numerical values given are representative but not necessarily realistic.

Context Title: 4.7  Interface Conditions for Chemical Species
Content: 4.7  Interface Conditions for Chemical Species
Victory Device also allows for species transport across interfaces provided that the involved 
species is deﬁned as mobile species (with a non-zero species diﬀusivity) in both adjacent 
regions (see Section 4.6.6 Heat Generation from Reactions).
Interface Species Continuity
By default, Victory Device assumes species continuity across the interface, which 
corresponds to the case that there is no barrier for the mobile species between the two regions.
Interface Species Wall
One can also assume no species transport across the interface by setting the ﬂag 
SPECIES.WALL together with the corresponding species name (SPECIES.NAME) on the 
INTERFACE statement. For example:
INTERFACE S.I SPECIES.NAME="H" SPECIES.WALL
Interface Species Barrier

interface model can be enabled by setting the ﬂag SPECIES.BARRIER. The thermal barriers 
are deﬁned in the same way as the species reactions in regions. However, the forward and the 
reverse rate can only include one type of species (Cs) which must be speciﬁed by

Context Title: 4.9  Chemistry Simulation Types
Content: 4.9  Chemistry Simulation Types
Victory Device allows you to perform three types of chemistry simulations, respectively 
using frozen, equilibrium, and transient chemistry. Additionally, after obtaining a solution 
with any type of chemistry, you may perform a small-signal AC analysis.

Context Title: 4.9.1  Frozen Chemistry
Content: 4.9.1  Frozen Chemistry
In frozen chemistry, chemical species are present, but chemical reactions and species 
transport are suppressed. This is useful in two situations:
1.
To initialize the electrical state of a device before considering chemistry effects.
2.
In cases where electrical biases are varied on a time-scale much shorter than those for 
reactions and species transport.
As an example of the latter case, you might save a structure file representing the state of a 
transient simulation at a particular time, then later load that structure and do a steady-state 
simulation with frozen chemistry to investigate what the electrical characteristics of the 
device would be at that moment.
To perform a simulation using frozen chemistry, add the FREEZE.SPECIES flag to a steady-
state SOLVE statement. Frozen chemistry will be used only if the FREEZE.SPECIES flag is 
present.

Context Title: 4.9.2  Equilibrium Chemistry
Content: 4.9.2  Equilibrium Chemistry
In equilibrium chemistry, the chemical reaction and species transport equations are solved for 
their steady-state equilibrium values. When charged species are present, the chemical species 
equilibrium may or may not depend on the biases applied to the device.
To perform a simulation using equilibrium chemistry, use a steady-state SOLVE statement but 
do not add the FREEZE.SPECIES flag. You will generally perform at least one equilibrium 
solve before starting a transient simulation, because your initial transient should depart from 
some equilibrium state.

Context Title: 4.9.3  Transient Chemistry
Content: 4.9.3  Transient Chemistry
In transient chemistry, the chemical reaction and species transport equations are solved as the 
local species concentrations vary in time. Victory Device will use transient chemistry when 
chemical species are present and you issue a transient SOLVE statement.

Context Title: 4.10  Output of Chemical Species Data
Content: 4.10  Output of Chemical Species Data
Quantities of interest for chemical species include concentrations, initial concentrations 
(doping), occupation fractions for trapping species, and reaction/recombination rates. These 
quantities may be output to structure and log files as described below.

Context Title: 4.10.1  Structure File Output
Content: 4.10.1  Structure File Output
When a simulation includes chemical species, the species concentrations are written to any 
output structure file by default. The species doping is also written, if it is present. You can 
turn off this behavior by setting ^IONS on an OUTPUT statement. Species recombination rates 
will be written to the structure file if you set the U.SPECIES flag on an OUTPUT statement. 
Structure file outputs are produced for both named and generic species, without distinction.
